World.title: Gun issued to Customs official used in Ateneo de Zamboanga shooting
World.content:
SHOOTING. General view of Ateneo de Zamboanga University after a shooting that killed two people, in Zamboanga City on August 18, 2026.

Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno says the shooter’s father, a district commander at the Port of Zamboanga, has been relieved of his post

CEBU, Philippines – One of the guns used in the shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University (AdZU) on Tuesday morning, August 18, was issued by the Bureau of Customs (BOC) to the shooter’s father, the district commander at the Port of Zamboanga, Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno told Rappler.

“I had to relieve him immediately to have an impartial investigation,” Nepomuceno said.

The gun attack, which killed two students, including the shooter, occurred at AdZU’s junior high school campus along Tumaga-Lunzuran Road. Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Olaso said in an ANC interview that the shooter was armed with a high-caliber firearm and a handgun.

Nepomuceno confirmed that the handgun was agency-issued, while authorities were still checking whether the other firearm was also a government-issued weapon.

Police confirmed that the shooter, a minor, was carrying a 9mm pistol. According to their initial report, the shooter went to Room 404 and shot a 10th grader, then went to the third floor, shouted, and shot himself.

The initial police report also said authorities found another pistol inside the classroom where the victim’s body lay. The victim, according to the police, was instantly killed.

“Prior to this, our security team has been preparing for a simulation exercise precisely because we understand the value of keeping everyone, both our students and personnel, safe,” AdZU president Father Guillrey Anthony “Ernald” Andal told reporters on Tuesday.

The school shooting occurred only a month after the AdZU Grade School Department conducted Zamboanga City’s first full “Human-Induced Simulation Exercise” (SIMEX) on July 18. The exercise included a simulation of an active shooter incident.

Andal assured the public that the university would share information on the incident as soon as they are able to receive them.

Zamboanga City Police Office director Colonel Fidel Fortaleza Jr. said in a Tuesday press conference that they have cleared the area where the incident happened and that all students at the university have been accounted for.

“Wala na po threat at this time (There is no threat at this time),” Fortaleza said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Zamboanga school shooting: DepEd appeals for ‘compassion over clicks’
World.content:
The Department of Education urges the public to stop sharing misinformation and wait for facts from official sources

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Education (DepEd) has appealed to the public to stop sharing videos, photographs, or other sensitive materials on the recent shooting at the Ateneo de Zamboanga University (AdZU) where two students died.

“The circulation of such material may further compound the trauma of those directly affected and cause additional distress to their loved ones,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday, August 18.

DepEd reiterated their reminder not to share misinformation about the incident and called on the public to “rely only on verified information” from official sources. “Let us choose compassion over clicks. Our priority must be the safety, dignity, and healing of the affected school community.”

DepEd warlier said they were coordinating with mental health partners to provide psychological and psychosocial support to affected individuals.

AdZU suspended classes on Tuesday and declared Wednesday, August 19, as a day of mourning.

Two students, including the shooter, died. According to police report, both minors were armed with 9mm pistols.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development has also offered psychosocial support, saying counselors and social workers from their field office are “equipped” to provide such services.

“Bagamat naka-lockdown pa kanina ‘yung Ateneo de Zamboanga University, nakahanda ang aming mga social workers to provide psychosocial intervention. ‘Yung mental wellness first aid ang importante,” DSWD chief Rex Gatchalian told reporters on Tuesday.

(Although Ateneo de Zamboanga University is on lockdown, our social workers are ready to provide psychosocial intervention. The mental wellness first aid is important.) – Rappler.com

World.title: LTFRB chair Mendoza, OTC chief Guadiz suspended over LTO IT system
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Vigor Mendoza II and Teofilo Guadiz III, both former LTO chiefs, had allowed the continued use of the Stradcom Corporation-operated system alongside the government’s newer Land Transportation Management System

MANILA, Philippines – Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board Chairman Vigor Mendoza II and Office of Transportation Cooperatives chief Teofilo “Jojo” Guadiz III have been placed under six-month preventive suspension, the Office of the Ombudsman announced on Tuesday, August 18.

Mendoza and Guadiz, both former Land Transportation Office (LTO) chiefs, were suspended over their roles in allowing the continued use of the Stradcom Corporation-operated system alongside the government’s newer Land Transportation Management System (LTMS).

The parallel use resulted in motorists being charged an additional P13.3 billion in computer fees from 2019 to 2025, according to the Ombudsman’s order and a Commission on Audit (COA) report.

“The continued utilization of the LTO IT System by Guadiz and Mendoza demonstrates a patent disregard of established government policy and prior official directives intended to transition LTO operations to the LTMS,” the Ombudsman said in its ruling.

Mendoza and Guadiz said in separate statements that they respect the decision of the Office of the Ombudsman.

“This will be a good opportunity for me to prove it, and eventually clear my name, in the proper forum,” Mendoza said, adding that he has yet to see the official order.

Guadiz, for his part, said, “I remain confident that the evidence and the official records will show that the actions I took during my tenure as Chief of the Land Transportation Office were lawful, undertaken in good faith, and guided by my duty to serve the public interest.”

The two officials said they have yet to see the official order.

In April 2024, Rappler reported that the parallel use of the two systems enabled opportunities for fraud and cost motorists billions of pesos each year.

COA likewise flagged the continued parallel operation of the systems, saying it resulted in the “non-maximization of the benefits” expected from the LTMS project.

The audit agency found that motorists shouldered an “additional burden and expense” from computer fees charged by Stradcom, totaling P13,379,196,499.73 between 2019 and 2025.

How the old system continued

The government and Stradcom entered into a Build-Own-Operate Agreement in 1998 for the establishment and operation of computer systems and other infrastructure used to process LTO transactions nationwide.

The then-Department of Transportation and Communications issued Stradcom a Final Certificate of Acceptance in February 2003. Its original 10-year concession expired on February 10, 2013, but the arrangement was subsequently extended on a month-to-month basis.

In 2016, the LTO and Stradcom signed a Phase Out Agreement, allowing the old system to remain in use until the LTO had a fully operational replacement.

Two years later, in 2018, the government contracted a joint venture led by Dermalog Identification Systems GmbH to develop and deliver a new LTO core system, now known as the LTMS.

The LTO issued a certificate of project completion and final acceptance for the LTMS in 2021.

After its rollout, the LTMS became the government’s principal platform for vehicle registration, driver’s licensing, and other LTO transactions. The agency was supposed to gradually transition away from the Stradcom-operated system.

The Ombudsman, however, found that Guadiz and Mendoza continued to support the use of the old system.

During Guadiz’s stint as LTO chief in 2022, the Ombudsman said he “pushed for the continued use of the LTO IT System” and favored Stradcom. Guadiz reportedly said the old system “provides a better solution.”

In 2023, while Mendoza was LTO chief, he issued several memoranda that the Ombudsman said “effectively reviv[ed] and institutionaliz[ed]” the parallel use of the old system alongside the LTMS.

In January 2025, Mendoza also directed the processing of public utility vehicle registration renewals through the old system without requiring confirmation from the LTFRB.

In October 2025, Malacañang announced the reshuffling of top officials in key transportation agencies. Mendoza was assigned to LTFRB, succeeding Guadiz. Guadiz was appointed as OTC chairman.

In October 2023, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. suspended then-LTFRB chief Guadiz due to “alleged corruption under his leadership.” Barely a month later, he was reinstated to his post. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Wildlife Recovery Expands From Protection to Reintroduction
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is reporting continued growth in several rare ungulate populations while expanding programs to return animals that disappeared from parts of the country to their natural habitats. From Przewalski’s horses and kulans to the recent release of a tiger into the wild, conservation policy is moving beyond protecting surviving wildlife toward rebuilding populations and the ecosystems needed to sustain them.

According to 2025 wildlife census data released by Kazakhstan’s Ecology and Natural Resources Ministry, populations of several rare ungulates have continued to grow. The country recorded 1,240 Bukhara deer, 16,122 goitered gazelles, 4,702 kulans and 17,604 argali, reported the Central Asia Climate Foundation.

Saiga numbers have grown on an even larger scale. Kazakhstan’s three saiga populations totaled nearly 3.98 million animals in 2025, including 2.3 million in the Ural population, 1.6 million in the Betpak-Dala population and 78,000 in the Ustyurt population.

The figures illustrate one of the major changes in Kazakhstan’s conservation agenda: protecting wildlife is no longer limited to preventing the disappearance of existing populations. The government is using reintroduction programs to restore species to areas where they had previously disappeared.

From protecting species to rebuilding populations

Reintroduction is a more complex process than simply releasing animals into the wild. For a population to survive, conservationists must ensure that suitable habitat, food sources and protection mechanisms already exist. This approach is visible in several of Kazakhstan’s current programs.

In the Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve in the Kostanai Region, the Center for the Reintroduction of Wild Ungulates, established in 2017, currently holds 14 Przewalski‘s horses, including 12 mares and two stallions. Kazakhstan plans to bring an additional 40 horses to the country by the end of 2029.

The program is part of a broader effort to restore a species that disappeared from Kazakhstan’s wild landscapes. Its significance therefore lies not only in increasing the number of animals held in the country, but ultimately in establishing a population capable of surviving in its historical habitat.

Kazakhstan is pursuing a similar strategy with kulans. A total of 66 animals have been relocated as part of population restoration efforts, including 42 to the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve and 24 to Altyn Dala.

The reintroduction of large herbivores can also have consequences beyond the survival of individual species. Ungulates are part of wider food chains and ecosystems, meaning their restoration can help create the ecological conditions necessary for other wildlife to return.

The tiger project tests an ecosystem-based approach

Perhaps the most ambitious example of this strategy is Kazakhstan’s program to return tigers to the country more than 70 years after they disappeared. The Turanian tiger vanished from Kazakhstan in the mid-20th century amid the destruction of tugai forests, hunting and the decline of its prey base. Kazakhstan is now using Amur tigers, considered the closest living genetic relatives of the extinct Turanian subspecies, as part of the restoration effort.

The Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve has become the main site for the project. Before the release of tigers, authorities spent years preparing the ecosystem, including reintroducing prey species such as kulans, goitered gazelles and wild boars.

That sequence is significant. Rather than beginning with the predator itself, the program first focused on rebuilding the ecological foundation needed to support it. The tiger project could therefore become an important test of whether Kazakhstan’s conservation programs can progress from increasing animal numbers to restoring functioning ecosystems.

Rare animals increasingly become indicators of ecosystem health

Other recent observations highlight the importance of long-term monitoring. In July, inspectors at Charyn State National Nature Park captured images of a Pallas’s cat, a rare and highly elusive predator listed in Kazakhstan’s Red Book.

A camera trap in Kolsai Lakes National Park also recorded several times a Tien Shan brown bear, another Red Book-listed species. Park authorities said the observation confirmed the continued presence of the bears within the protected area.

In Altyn-Emel National Park, winter counts conducted in February monitored populations of kulan, goitered gazelle and argali. The park also provides habitat for species including the snow leopard, lynx, bear and Pallas’s cat.

Such observations are important because population figures alone do not provide a complete picture of conservation success. A growing number of animals can indicate that protection measures are working, but the longer-term question is whether habitats remain capable of supporting those populations as they expand.

A larger conservation challenge

Kazakhstan is home to 835 species of vertebrates, according to the Ecology Ministry, including 178 species of mammals and 489 species of birds. Around 132 species and subspecies of vertebrates and 96 species of invertebrates are classified as rare or endangered.

The recovery of individual populations is therefore only one part of a much broader conservation challenge. The recent growth in saiga numbers and the continued presence of rare species in national parks show the potential results of sustained protection. At the same time, the expansion of reintroduction programs for Przewalski’s horses, kulans and tigers represents a more demanding next stage.

The difference is between protecting what remains and restoring what has been lost. For Kazakhstan, the next challenge may therefore be to connect successful protection of individual species with the restoration of larger ecosystems.

World.title: Air Astana Extends Dubai Flight Cancellations Through Sept. 30
World.content:
ALMATY – Air Astana has extended the cancellation of flights to Dubai from Almaty and Astana through Sept. 30 due to the continuing unstable situation in the Persian Gulf region.

The airline said its flight schedule for October has also been adjusted, with the frequency of flights on these routes reduced. Passengers affected by the cancellations can rebook free of charge in the same booking class on flights operating until Nov. 20, 2026.

Alternatively, passengers can receive a full refund at their original point of purchase or change their tickets free of charge to other international Air Astana destinations, paying any applicable fare difference.

World.title: Astana Finance Days 2026 to Bring Global Investors and Financial Leaders to Kazakhstan
World.content:
ALMATY – More than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries are expected to gather in Kazakhstan’s capital on Sept. 9-10 for the ninth Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 forum, hosted by the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).

The forum will bring together investors, representatives of the financial and technology sectors, regulators, government and quasi-state institutions, and international businesses. Since its launch in 2018, Astana Finance Days has developed into one of the region’s major financial forums, providing a platform for discussions on capital markets, investment and financial cooperation.

The 2026 program will focus on capital markets and investment products, regulation and market confidence, institutional innovation, financing the real economy, and regional and cross-border capital cooperation.

Confirmed speakers include Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov, Association of Financiers of Kazakhstan Chairperson Yelena Bakhmutova and Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States Kubanychbek Omuraliev.

Representatives from international financial institutions and global companies are also expected to participate, including the Islamic Development Bank Institute, Freedom Holding, Binance, Mastercard, Bloomberg and the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

The forum will feature the AFD Exhibition, bringing together financial institutions, banks, investment and asset management companies, as well as fintech and technology projects. According to the AIFC, the event will provide participants with opportunities to discuss global financial trends, explore investment and business opportunities, and establish contacts with investors, company executives and industry leaders.

The forum will also highlight business development opportunities within the AIFC ecosystem, featuring case studies on company growth, capital raising and expansion into international markets.

For Kazakhstan, which is seeking to strengthen its position as a financial hub connecting Central Asia with global markets, the forum provides an opportunity to bring global investors and financial institutions into closer contact with the region.

World.title: How Kazakhstan’s First Released Tiger Adapts to Life in Wild
World.content:
ALMATY – Umit, the female Amur tiger released into the wild in Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on July 31, is continuing to explore the region’s forests and habitats near water as specialists monitor her adaptation to life in the wild.

According to the Forestry and Wildlife Committee of the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, specialists are tracking the tiger through GPS monitoring, field observations and camera traps. The combined monitoring system allows researchers to follow Umit’s movements and activity remotely while also studying tracks and other signs of her behavior and interaction with the surrounding environment.

Umit is currently exploring the nearby areas, locations near water and habitats inhabited by wild animals as she gradually adapts to her new environment. The information collected on her movements, activity and behavior will help specialists assess how the adaptation process develops over time.

Umit’s release marked the first return of a tiger to Kazakhstan’s wild after more than 70 years of absence. The tiger was released as part of the country’s longer-term tiger restoration program in the Ile-Balkhash region.

Earlier, The Astana Times reported on how tigers disappeared from Kazakhstan and the efforts undertaken to restore the conditions necessary for their return. The release of Umit represents an important early stage of that effort, with her adaptation to the reserve now providing scientists with an opportunity to assess how a tiger introduced into the restored habitat navigates and uses the landscape.

As monitoring continues, Umit’s movements will offer one of the first real-world tests of Kazakhstan’s broader ambition to restore a viable tiger population in the region.

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens 5.2 Million Hectares for Carbon Projects. Will Investors Follow?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has identified 5.2 million hectares of non-forested land within its 31-million-hectare state forest fund as having potential for carbon projects, opening new opportunities for investors in emissions reduction and carbon absorption projects, Ecology and Natural Resources Minister Yerlan Nyssanbayev said.

“This opens new opportunities for investors to participate in projects to reduce and absorb emissions and generate carbon units,” Nyssanbayev said at a seminar on developing Kazakhstan’s carbon project market under the Paris Agreement.

The opportunity comes as Kazakhstan seeks to attract climate investment while meeting its international commitments. The country has pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 15% by 2030 and 17% by 2035, compared with 1990 levels, reported Kazinform on Aug. 13.

According to Nyssanbayev, the country’s potential is concentrated in forestry, agriculture and energy efficiency. The government is also considering Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as an additional mechanism for attracting investment in emission-reduction and carbon-absorption projects.

Nyssanbayev previously told The Astana Times that developing carbon sequestration sites could help restore degraded pasturelands, expand green areas and increase carbon absorption. He also noted that such sites could allow farmers to participate in the carbon market through carbon farming.

The move is significant because Kazakhstan’s existing greenhouse gas regulation system, including the free allocation of emission quotas, does not provide sufficient incentives for technological modernization, the minister said.

A clearer framework for investors

A revised version of Kazakhstan’s rules on state regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and absorption entered into force on Aug. 10. The changes establish detailed procedures for climate projects under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

The updated rules define key concepts, including validation, verification, monitoring, authorization, baseline scenarios and internationally transferable mitigation outcomes. They also establish the process for transferring verified emission-reduction or absorption results internationally.

Participation in Article 6 mechanisms is voluntary. Developers must first submit a project concept for review by relevant government authorities. If approved, the project proceeds to registration and preparation of project, monitoring and sustainable-development plans.

The documents then undergo validation and examination. After implementation, project results are monitored and verified before being recorded in the relevant registry.

International transfer requires separate authorization. Project approval therefore does not automatically allow investors to transfer all future results abroad; each subsequent reporting period requires new verification and authorization.

The new framework gives investors a clearer route from project development to internationally transferable carbon units. However, land availability alone will not determine whether the market develops. Reliable monitoring, transparent verification, predictable approval procedures and the ability to demonstrate genuine emission reductions or increased carbon absorption will also be important.

Why the market matters for exporters

Kazakhstan’s carbon market could also become increasingly important for companies trading with the European Union. Kazakhstan’s aluminum, iron and steel sectors are among those most exposed to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which puts a carbon cost on certain imports.

The International Trade Center has estimated that accurate emissions monitoring and reporting could significantly reduce potential CBAM costs for Kazakh exporters. Strengthening domestic carbon pricing and verification systems could therefore serve two purposes: attract investment into climate projects while helping businesses adapt to stricter international carbon requirements.

For Kazakhstan, the next test will be whether the new rules can turn the country’s large land and emissions-reduction potential into credible projects that attract investment, generate verifiable carbon units and support the country’s climate commitments.

World.title: Beyond Oil: Why New Resources Will Decide Global Power
World.content:
While the prevalent discourse in the 20th century centered on the importance of oil pipelines, gaining access to oil reserves and spotlighting countries controlling energy supplies ranging from OPEC states to European giants such as Norway for economic resilience, the current, global, geopolitical environment points to a new trend.

Supply side shocks impacting the international energy market due to militarization of strategic maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab El Mandeb Strait, is shifting attention towards countries controlling materials essential for powering domestic industries clean energy transitions, defense equipment, transistors, integrated circuits, diodes and solar cells. Regions less reliant on oil but have deposits of lithium, processing facilities, rare earths, copper reserves and uranium deposits are now increasingly relevant as this translates into greater strategic and economic influence.

Competition between the EU and China on the electrical vehicles front requires access to nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths whereas renewable energy systems warrant aluminum, silicon and rare earth magnets to sustain a workable ecosystem. Advanced electronics also require materials such as gallium and germanium whereas military industrial complexes seeking to counter adversaries need specialized minerals for aircrafts, radar systems, reconnaissance equipment and satellites. As a result, critical minerals are increasingly tied to national security.

The International Atomic Energy Agency in its recent Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 for example, underlines demand for minerals powering clean energy technologies growing exponentially in the next few decades as supply chains remain incredibly constrained and limited to certain economic regions. As per the IEA’s 2026 assessments, demand for lithium is projected to more than triple by 2040, which benefits countries such as China who dominate processing and refining of critical minerals. However, lessons from increased dependence on oil underlines an irrefutable fact- countries which rely on a few suppliers risk facing strategic challenges as supply chains remain volatile.

In light of this, Central Asia gains traction as a potential hub for global supply chain management. Kazakhstan for example remains one of the world’s largest uranium producers with extensive reserves of zinc and titanium alongside lithium and chromium at its disposal. The country’s national atomic corporation, Kazatomprom places Astana’s global uranium production in 2025 at 39% while accounting for 20% of global supplies. These unique advantages can be capitalized on if investments in refining, manufacturing, processing, research and technology to build domestic industrial capacities and support domestic resource bases become more pronounced.

Sitting at the confluence of Russia, China, Europe, the Middle East and South Asia the entire region is also a potential node for regional connectivity where minerals can aid supply chain management as an alternative to riskier routes. This includes the Middle Corridor for diversification of supply chains where the Trans Caspian International Transport Route continues to gain coverage in key policy circles ranging from capitals such as London to Beijing to address bottlenecks from reliance on maritime chokepoints in the Middle East.

However, mineral deposits prove valuable only if they manage to reach international markets.

This warrants the avoidance of the ‘resource trap’ in the current, global, geopolitical environment. Cases such as the Democratic Republic of Congo in Africa quintessentially point at how lack of requisite infrastructure and targeted investments can prevent realization of true economic potential. While Central Asia’s case differs significantly, indigenization remains the key. Selling of copper ores for example, while importing finished products creates economic imbalances domestically which can only be addressed if production of copper components for finished products indigenously is achieved. Similarly, developing relevant knowledge on nuclear technology to channelize uranium ore deposits is the correct approach for domestic prosperity amid increased global demand. For Central Asian states, this requires investments in advanced mining technologies, partnerships with countries specializing in producing finished commodities, development of human capital and institutional collaborations.

Yet despite challenges, few can doubt that Central Asia can act as a bridge particularly as global competition for minerals heats up ranging from the United States to Europe, seeking to invest in domestic capacities and build partnerships with resource rich states to counter China on battery supply chains and rare earth technologies. The Trump administration for example, is treating access to critical minerals as tied with issues of US national security. What is commendable is that from Uzbekistan to the Kyrgyz Republic, all five states alongside Azerbaijan have adopted multi vector, multipronged foreign policies in the absence of camp politics which allows the region to position itself as a credible, reliable supplier and a partner in technological development.

For the region, this constitutes an opportunity in 2026 to move beyond being a mere supplier of resources to becoming a key driver of the global economy provided that targeted investments take place to convert natural resources into innovation and economic resilience.

The author is Hamzah Rifaat, the president of Initiate Futures, a policy think tank. He is also an author for the Trends Group in Abu Dhabi and is cooperating with Nightingale Int.

World.title: From Illicit Wealth to Public Services: Where Kazakhstan’s Recovered Assets Are Going
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has returned 1.154 trillion tenge (US$2.5 billion) in assets to state ownership since launching its asset-recovery program in September 2023. The central question now is how effectively these funds can be converted into long-term public benefits, particularly in regions facing infrastructure shortages.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has repeatedly stressed that the asset-recovery process should serve a broader public purpose.

“The restoration of social justice through the return of illegally acquired assets is not a matter of political expediency or a PR campaign, but a principled position of the state,” Tokayev said in a Jan. 5 interview with the Turkistan newspaper.

The funds are channeled through the Special State Fund, created to finance social and infrastructure projects. According to the General Prosecutor’s Office, 617.6 billion tenge (US$1.3 billion) has been allocated to 466 projects, with water supply, healthcare and education accounting for the largest share. The scale and geographic distribution of this spending indicate that asset recovery is becoming not only a legal and fiscal process, but also a mechanism for addressing regional infrastructure gaps.

From recovered assets to public infrastructure

Of the 1.154 trillion tenge returned, 1.044 trillion tenge (US$2.3 billion) is in cash, while the remainder consists of real estate, company shares, land and other assets. Annual returns increased sharply from 302.5 billion tenge (US$653.9 million) in 2024 to 773.7 billion tenge (US$1.67 billion) in 2025. The fund returned a further 77.7 billion tenge (US$167.9 million) this year.

The Special State Fund has allocated financing for 235 water-supply projects, 190 healthcare facilities, 17 education projects, 11 infrastructure projects, seven transport facilities and six sports facilities, reported Kazinform on Aug. 17.

Implementation has already moved beyond the allocation stage. More than 253 billion tenge (US$546.9 million) has been spent on 364 projects, of which 349 have been commissioned. Completed projects include 188 water-supply facilities, 163 healthcare facilities, seven education facilities, three sports facilities, one transport facility and two infrastructure projects.

The figures show that the program is producing physical assets, but they also highlight an important implementation issue: the impact of returned funds will depend on whether projects address persistent local infrastructure deficits and remain operational over the long term.

Where the money is going

Eastern Kazakhstan received the largest allocation at 78.9 billion tenge (US$170.5 million), followed by North Kazakhstan with 69.4 billion tenge (US$150 million) and Astana with 64.7 billion tenge (US$139.8 million). The lowest allocations went to Shymkent, the Atyrau Region and the Mangystau Region.

These differences do not necessarily reflect a region’s size or economic importance. According to the General Prosecutor’s Office, allocations depend on the number of applications submitted by local authorities, the availability of completed design and cost documentation, project priorities and the severity of infrastructure shortages.

This makes project preparation an important factor in determining access to financing. Regions with clearly prepared projects and pressing infrastructure needs are better positioned to receive funding.

The National Budget Commission decides how funds are distributed. Once financing is approved, projects are implemented under Kazakhstan’s budget legislation and subject to financial control, state audit and treasury procedures.

What to watch next

The program’s success will depend not only on the amount recovered, but on how well the money is used. Key measures will be completed projects, better infrastructure and improved access to essential services.

The long-term goal is to ensure that recovered funds reach regions with the greatest needs and improve people’s quality of life.

World.title: Kazakhstan Deepens University Ties with Japan and South Korea
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding academic and scientific cooperation with leading universities and research institutions in Japan and South Korea. The country seeks to strengthen higher education, research and artificial intelligence (AI) development.

During visits to Seoul and Tokyo in August, Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek met with university leaders and government officials to discuss academic partnerships, joint research, faculty and student exchanges, and workforce development.

Strengthening ties with Japan

In Tokyo, Nurbek held talks with the leadership of Tokyo Metropolitan University and the United Nations University (UNU).

During a meeting with Tokyo Metropolitan University President Takaya Ohashi, the two sides discussed expanding university partnerships, increasing academic mobility and launching joint educational and research projects. Nurbek also invited Ohashi to attend the Strategic Partners Forum, scheduled for November in Astana.

Cooperation with the UNU was another focus of the visit. During talks with the university’s Rector and U.N. Under-Secretary-General Tshilidzi Marwala, the officials discussed expanding collaboration in science, higher education, research and sustainable development.

The two sides also explored ways to expand the university’s presence in Kazakhstan, in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to strengthen international academic partnerships. Marwala accepted an invitation to attend the Strategic Partners Forum in Astana.

The visit builds on growing educational cooperation between Kazakhstan and Japan following Tokayev’s official visit to Tokyo for the inaugural Central Asia-Japan Summit in December 2025. During the summit, Tokayev described human capital as “the main engine of development” and invited Japanese universities to establish branches and educational centers in Kazakhstan.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Japan’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan Yasumasa Iijima said that educational cooperation has become an increasingly important pillar of bilateral relations alongside trade and investment.

Kazakhstan’s efforts to expand international academic partnerships come as the country strengthens its position as Central Asia’s leading higher education hub. In July, Almaty reached its highest-ever position in the QS Best Student Cities 2027 ranking, while the country recorded another year of growth in international student enrollment.

AI partnership with South Korea

In Seoul, Nurbek met South Korea’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon.

The discussions focused on expanding cooperation in science, higher education and AI, including technology transfer, joint research and the training of highly qualified specialists.

One of the key topics was the planned opening of a branch campus of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) in Kazakhstan.

Nurbek also met with KAIST Vice President Jaemin Jung to discuss academic exchanges, joint research projects and cooperation in AI and digital technologies.

Separate meetings with the leadership of Seoul National University and Korea University focused on expanding collaboration in medicine, engineering, information technology and other priority fields. Both universities maintain partnerships with Kazakh higher education institutions.

Educational cooperation between Kazakhstan and South Korea is also expanding through dual-degree programs.

Seoul Cyber University currently partners with Q University, Almaty Humanitarian and Economic University, and Maqsut Narikbayev University (MNU). The expanding partnerships reflect Kazakhstan’s ambition to become a regional hub for AI and digital innovation.

The visits come as Kazakhstan and South Korea deepen broader strategic ties. Earlier this month, Tokayev accepted an invitation to visit Seoul during talks with South Korean Presidential Chief of Staff Kang Hoon-sik.

South Korea has also become an increasingly popular study destination for Kazakh students. According to the Korean Educational Development Institute, 1,516 Kazakh students were enrolled at South Korean universities as of April 1, 2024.

The trend reflects broader educational cooperation between the two countries. Earlier this year, Woosong University opened a branch campus in Turkistan, while exchange partnerships continue to expand across multiple institutions.

World.title: ‘Work is being carried out to international standards’ — Georgia’s Gelati Monastery Rehabilitation Committee responds to criticism
World.content:
Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati has described reports circulating on social media and in the media about conservation work at the monastery as disinformation.

The committee said the disinformation was harming efforts to restore Gelati.

The Gelati Monastery complex is one of Georgia’s most important medieval cultural and religious monuments. King David IV, known as David the Builder, founded it in 1106.

The complex’s main church is the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. In medieval Georgia, Gelati was not only a monastery but also an important centre of education and scholarship, home to the renowned Gelati Academy.

Recent reports and assessments have raised concerns about the condition of Gelati. The debate has focused on several issues:

The church’s temporary roof, which critics have called “cellophane”;

The risk of frescoes collapsing;

Mould and condensation inside the church;

The condition of the drainage system;

Plans to install an underfloor heating system;

Cooperation with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure;

The condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

What does the committee say?

The committee rejects claims that the Gelati Cathedral is covered with “cellophane”. According to the committee, the creation of a single temporary covering for the cathedral was one of the main requirements set by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre as early as 2020.

The committee says Georgian and German specialists jointly designed the roof. The authorities approved the project after considering several proposals. The covering uses a high-tech PVC-based material made in Germany specifically for Gelati. According to the committee, the material meets international conservation standards.

The committee also rejects reports of widespread loss of frescoes inside the cathedral. It says all critically damaged areas have been stabilised, while conservation work on the wall paintings is continuing in stages.

The statement also addresses Gelati’s historic drainage system. According to the committee, drainage channels built during the reign of David the Builder stopped functioning in 1510 after Ottoman forces burned the monastery. The committee says archaeological excavations also support this conclusion.

“For centuries, the drainage system was filled with earth, ash and coal,” the committee said.

The committee also responded to criticism over humidity and condensation inside the church. According to the committee, Italian professor Dario Camuffo conducted the study of Gelati’s microclimate. The committee considers him one of the recognised experts in the study of the microclimate of cultural heritage sites.

The committee explained that the problem at Gelati stems from the church’s massive walls, which retain the cold for a long time during winter. In spring, when outdoor temperatures rise and warm air enters the church, condensation can form on the walls and floor.

Camuffo suggested gradually heating the floor as one possible solution. However, the committee stressed that this remains a working hypothesis and requires further research before a final decision.

The committee also clarified the memorandum it signed with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure. According to the committee, the “pilot restoration” provided for in the document does not mean conducting experiments at Gelati. Instead, it refers to pilot or trial restoration work, which is standard international practice.

“This is a widely accepted standard for restoring wall paintings. Before treating an entire fresco, conservators test the safety of the proposed conservation methods on a small, less visible area. Only after obtaining a positive result do they begin the full-scale process,” the committee said.

In a significant part of its statement, the committee also responded to critics and addressed allegations about the condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

According to the committee, experts already knew about the poor condition of the mosaics in 1989. The claim is based on an assessment by restorer Carlo Bakuradze at the time, who found that about 85% of the mosaic depicting the Virgin Mary had detached from its base.

The committee also criticised specialists who question the ongoing conservation work and reminded them of their own responsibility for Gelati’s condition in the past.

“It is cynical and hypocritical for people to question the quality of conservation work when, under their direct supervision, extensive water-infiltration problems emerged within just one year at the recently built Bagrati Cathedral — problems that persist to this day,” the statement said. The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati urged critics not to try to damage the reputation of the ongoing work and to act according to professional ethics.

“We call on those pursuing certain subjective goals and agendas to refrain from attempts to discredit the conservation work carried out under the Gelati rehabilitation programme and deliberately mislead the public. We also call on them to return to the standards of common decency and professional ethics,” the committee said.

The committee concluded by stressing again that the work at the Gelati Monastery complex is unprecedented in scale, involves international experts and meets international conservation standards.

What happened at Gelati?

The main problem at Gelati Monastery is water and dampness, which have damaged the church’s wall paintings and mosaics over time. The situation became particularly serious after restoration work in recent years, including problems with the roof.

The problem became so serious that the UNESCO World Heritage Centre and its advisory bodies issued specific recommendations to Georgia. The authorities changed their approach to the restoration work in response to those recommendations and established the current Rehabilitation Committee.

A ruling by Georgia’s Supreme Court also notes that workers carried out roofing work at Gelati without an adequate expert assessment. The court found that problems with the materials used and the quality of the installation created a real risk of water entering the building.

Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

World.title: Suicides in Armenia’s military: the statistics and debate over who should be held responsible
World.content:
Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

In Armenia, debate continues over the causes of military deaths in peacetime and who should bear responsibility. A series of suicides has prompted the latest discussions. The first incident occurred on 21 July. Then, on 13 August, the Defence Ministry reported that it had found the body of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan with a gunshot wound. In both cases, the Investigative Committee said it had opened criminal proceedings under the article on negligent incitement to suicide.

According to the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, this was the 31st military death in Armenia in 2026. However, the Defence Ministry says 11 servicemen have died. Moreover, the ministry’s spokesperson said the number of military deaths had become the subject of various forms of manipulation.

“We often see reports in the press about 30 deaths in the army over the course of a year. But no one says how many of those 30 cases actually occurred in the army, which were related to military service and which were not. Even if the deaths were related to service, were all of them murders and suicides?” Aram Torosyan said, calling for greater precision.

Government bodies and civil society organisations also differ over who should bear responsibility for military deaths. Human rights groups tend to argue that the defence minister and the chief of the General Staff should be held accountable. However, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan does not share this view.

“In my assessment, it is not the case that the chief of the General Staff and the defence minister are failing to make sufficient efforts to address this issue,” Nikol Pashinyan said.

Civil society data differs from official figures

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan, who represents the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, said she had seen no positive changes. According to her, the number of military deaths in non-combat situations has not decreased:

“The situation is even worse than in 2025. There were 35 deaths throughout 2025, while there have already been 31 cases in the first eight months of this year.”

She stressed that 10 cases in 2025 were classified as related to military service, while the same number have been recorded in just eight months this year.

Defence Ministry spokesman Aram Torosyan says these claims do not match the official statistics.

“We have recorded 11 deaths this year. Only five of those who died were serving their mandatory military service. Some died from illness, while others died in a mine explosion,” he said.

Torosyan said six of the 11 deaths involved suicide or incitement to suicide, but only three were related to military service.

Commenting on last year’s figures, he stressed that there were no cases of murder in the army in 2025.

Causes of suicides in the army

The authorities have not released details about the death of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan. However, the prime minister said that 85-90% of suicides in the army result from:

gambling addiction and the debts it causes;

personal and family problems;

servicemen falling asleep while on duty, which can lead to conflicts with fellow soldiers.

“If a serviceman on duty at a border post falls asleep, he puts other people’s lives at risk. Soldiers then begin to treat the person who fell asleep at the post negatively, and he becomes isolated. After returning from combat duty, psychological pressure can also follow. We should not place all the blame on the army leadership. I am responsible for the fact that we have still not found a solution to this problem,” Pashinyan said.

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan believes that the first two causes mentioned by the prime minister have nothing to do with the army. At the same time, she believes authorities can eliminate the third factor by taking systemic measures:

“Why does a serviceman fall asleep while on duty? Are there enough personnel to ensure that everyone gets enough rest and does not feel the need to sleep while on duty?”

Prime minister’s statements and dismissals

On the day the soldier died, Nikol Pashinyan told reporters that the government had discussed the situation and decided to make dismissals. He announced personnel changes in the Military Police and the Defence Ministry’s Department of Moral and Psychological Support:

“We will analyse in detail why our efforts in this area are not producing the desired results and draw conclusions. Yes, there must be individual accountability.”

The same day, reports emerged that Military Police chief Ashot Zakaryan had submitted his resignation. Today, the president dismissed Zakaryan from the post he had held for six years. In another decree, Major General Aram Hovhannisyan was appointed to replace him. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy interior minister and police chief.

There are no specific details yet about personnel changes in the Department of Moral and Psychological Support.

In recent days, the Defence Ministry has reported consultations on organising psychological support in the armed forces. To review a report on the psychological assistance provided to the military, the defence minister met professors from Yerevan State University’s Research Centre for Psychology. The ministry is also holding discussions with conscript sergeants and officers serving on duty at military posts.

“The agenda includes issues related to preventing hazing and eliminating inappropriate behaviour in the army,” the ministry said.

Comment

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan believes:

“The army’s top command, led by Suren Papikyan, must give the public a detailed explanation of the series of deaths.

Has anyone from the army’s top command visited the military unit to establish the circumstances of the soldier’s death and find out what was happening there? I strongly doubt it.

Papikyan did not even visit the military unit in the village of Azat when 15 servicemen died.

On 19 January 2023, a fire broke out in the engineering and sapper company’s premises in the village of Azat, killing 15 servicemen. Three others suffered burns of varying severity.

Then, as now, Nikol Pashinyan spoke on Papikyan’s behalf. He named those responsible and accountable. But he did not explain what the Military Police had to do with the death.

If Pashinyan knows more about the situation in the army and at military units, why is Papikyan still the defence minister?”

Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

World.title: White House: China is using Georgia to circumvent US tariffs
World.content:
US tariffs on China

According to a White House report titled The Great Transshipment Scam, China is using third countries, including Georgia, to circumvent US tariffs.

The Trump administration’s report names 40 countries and territories as participants in China’s “shadow shipping network”. The White House says these countries may have helped China circumvent US trade restrictions by transshipping and processing goods destined for the US.

The report divides the economies into three categories:

The first category includes countries and trading blocs that receive significant volumes of China-linked goods but have diversified industrial markets. The White House places Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, Mexico, South Korea and Taiwan in this group.

The second category includes countries with significant economic integration with China. According to the report, these are Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam.

The third category includes China’s “secondary targets”. The White House considers this group to include relatively small economies such as Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Argentina, Switzerland, Panama, Colombia, Chile, Cambodia and the United Arab Emirates.

According to the report, rerouting Chinese goods through third countries is one of the mechanisms companies use to avoid US tariffs on Chinese imports.

The White House published the report as part of the broader trade policy of the US administration. One of its main goals is to tighten enforcement of restrictions on imports from China and prevent companies from circumventing tariffs through third countries.

In 2025, Georgia imported $1.98 billion worth of goods from China, while its exports to the US amounted to just $120 million.

The value of goods imported from China into Georgia was significantly higher than the value of Georgian exports to the US. According to 2025 data, ferroalloys accounted for the largest category of goods imported from China into Georgia.

During the same period, Georgia’s main exports to the US included power-generating equipment and passenger cars.

Trade data show that Chinese imports account for a significant share of Georgia’s trade with China, while Georgian exports to the US remain relatively small.

US President Donald Trump began imposing and gradually increasing tariffs on Chinese goods in February 2025. By April 2025, the rate had reached 145%. Beijing responded with similar measures, imposing a 125% tariff on US products.

Following talks in May that year, the US cut the newly imposed tariffs from 145% to 30%, while China reduced its tariffs from 125% to 10%. However, other tariffs introduced before 2025 remained in place.

According to data published by the US Congress, various tariffs on Chinese goods are currently in effect under several US laws. Some target China directly, while others apply to specific economic sectors and also affect Chinese goods.

US tariffs on China

World.title: Deportation, ‘international wanted list’ mark new escalation in Baku-Moscow tensions
World.content:
Escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations

Two developments on 17 August highlighted the continuing fragility of relations between Baku and Moscow. Russia deported Bakhtiyar Hasanov, chairman of the Azerbaijani National-Cultural Autonomy in Moscow, to Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan, in turn, placed three Russian citizens on an international wanted list: Moscow 24 TV presenter Ivan Knyazev, political consultant and media expert Semyon Uralov, and journalist and adviser to the Russian transport minister Alexei Chadayev.

The fact that the two developments occurred on the same day may at first suggest that they were reciprocal measures. However, the process that culminated in Hasanov’s deportation had begun well before 17 August, with his case under consideration for at least several months. Therefore, while there is no public evidence of a direct causal link between the two decisions, both developments fit into the broader pattern of the prolonged deterioration in Azerbaijani-Russian relations.

Deportation of Bakhtiyar Hasanov

According to open sources, Bakhtiyar Hasanov was detained in Russia in June 2026 and placed in a temporary detention centre for foreign nationals. He appealed against the decision to deport him, but the court rejected his appeal.

According to sources, Hasanov’s Russian citizenship was revoked in September 2025. In autumn 2025, the Agentstvo media outlet established that Hasanov’s passport, issued in 2019, was listed as invalid in a Russian government database. Hasanov himself denied at the time that he had been stripped of his citizenship.

One of the key questions is the legal basis on which his citizenship was revoked. Open sources provide no complete or unequivocal explanation for the decision.

The case also carries political significance because of Hasanov’s status. For many years, he cooperated with official Moscow bodies dealing with diaspora and interethnic relations and served on public councils. His deportation is therefore also being viewed as part of a broader trend of pressure on the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia.

Growing pressure on the diaspora

Since the summer of 2025, several prominent members of the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia have been stripped of their citizenship, detained or expelled from the country. The names of Arshad Khankishiyev, Elshan Ibrahimov and Javid Rzayev have been mentioned in this context.

Russian nationalist and Kremlin-aligned media have largely portrayed these measures as part of efforts to combat illegal migration, alleged links to criminal groups and security concerns. However, final court rulings on all the allegations made against these individuals are not publicly available.

This process took on a more overtly political dimension following an operation targeting Azerbaijani families in Yekaterinburg in June 2025. The deaths of the Safarov brothers during the operation prompted a sharp reaction from Baku. Moscow linked the operation to an investigation into crimes committed many years earlier, while the Azerbaijani side focused on reports of violence and torture against those detained.

Since then, the issue of the diaspora has gradually moved beyond the social and cultural sphere and become one of the instruments of political pressure in relations between the two countries.

Baku’s charges against three Russian citizens

On 17 August, Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office said that Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev had been placed on a wanted list as part of a criminal investigation.

The investigation relates to programmes published on Uralov’s YouTube channel on 14 July and 13 August. According to the Azerbaijani authorities, the broadcasts contained calls for the violent overthrow of the country’s constitutional order, violations of its territorial integrity, terrorist activity and incitement of ethnic hatred.

The criminal case is being investigated under Articles 214-2, 281.2 and 283.2.1 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code. A court ordered the three men to be detained in absentia.

Excerpts from the broadcasts published by Azerbaijani media include remarks about a possible military operation against Baku, military pressure on Azerbaijan from the Caspian Sea and the use of physical violence against the country’s leadership. However, the Prosecutor General’s Office has not published full transcripts of the broadcasts, expert assessments or all the episodes on which the charges are based.

What do Uralov and Chadayev say?

The accused reject Baku’s allegations. Alexei Chadayev denied inciting ethnic hatred, saying that his criticism was directed not against the Azerbaijani people but against the country’s political leadership.

Semyon Uralov, for his part, described the Azerbaijani authorities’ decision as politically motivated. In subsequent Telegram posts, he continued to sharply criticise the political systems of post-Soviet countries, including the Azerbaijani authorities.

The response indicates that the case has moved beyond the legal sphere and become part of the broader information confrontation between the two countries.

‘International wanted list’ does not mean automatic arrest

The term “international wanted list”, used by Azerbaijani media, does not mean that a wanted person will automatically be arrested in another country.

Even if Interpol issues a Red Notice, it does not constitute an international arrest warrant. Each country decides whether to detain a wanted person in accordance with its own laws. In addition, Interpol’s constitution prohibits the organisation from intervening in matters of a political, military, religious or racial character.

The outcome of Baku’s request will therefore depend on the legal evidence submitted, as well as on how other countries assess the case — as a criminal prosecution or as a continuation of the political confrontation.

Ukraine factor

The latest escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations comes against the backdrop of the growing prominence of the Ukraine issue.

On 6 August, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov made his first official visit to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and visited Irpin. Azerbaijan reiterated its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying Azerbaijani gas to Ukraine.

Against this political backdrop, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko visited Baku on 16–17 August and met Ilham Aliyev. The presentation to Aliyev of a certificate naming him an honorary citizen of Irpin could be perceived in Moscow as a symbolic political gesture.

There is no evidence confirming a direct link between these developments and Hasanov’s deportation. However, the Azerbaijani leadership’s increasingly open articulation of a position on Ukraine that differs from Moscow’s fits into the broader picture of growing discontent in Russian political circles.

New mechanisms of mutual pressure

One notable change in relations between Baku and Moscow over the past two years has been the increasingly active use of law-enforcement and administrative mechanisms in the context of their political confrontation.

Russia has applied citizenship and migration laws, as well as criminal legislation, against members of the Azerbaijani diaspora. Azerbaijan, in turn, has used criminal prosecution mechanisms against individuals linked to Russian media over statements that Baku regards as posing a threat to the country.

This does not in itself mean that the legal arguments put forward by either side are unfounded. However, the fact that such legal measures are being taken against the backdrop of political crises in bilateral relations inevitably raises questions about their selective application and possible use for political purposes.

Where are relations heading?

At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: Prosecutor says former deputy economy minister Mikautadze gave bribe to ex-security chief Liluashvili
World.content:
Corruption cases in Georgia

Prosecutor Mariam Berdzenishvili said former deputy economy minister Romeo Mikautadze was supposed to go to the State Security Service and personally hand over the money to its former head, Grigol Liluashvili. She said the money was delivered to Liluashvili’s office. Berdzenishvili told reporters this before a court hearing in the case against Grigol Liluashvili.

According to the prosecutor, Mikautadze, who testified as a witness in the case, told the court that he underwent a security check and other required procedures when he entered the State Security Service (SSS) building. He then went to Liluashvili’s office.

Berdzenishvili said the investigation also has other evidence supporting the accuracy and reliability of the information provided by Mikautadze. In particular, investigators questioned a businessman who, according to the prosecutor, gave the court virtually the same account as Mikautadze.

She said the investigation requested data from the relevant companies covering the period when Mikautadze allegedly handed the money to Liluashvili. Berdzenishvili said an analysis of mobile phone data and internet traffic showed that the two men were in the same place at the same time.

“The prosecution also requested documents relating to the alleged handover of the bribe,” she added.

The prosecutor said the case contains direct evidence supported by other materials, and that there are no objective grounds to question its credibility.

Berdzenishvili said the defence argument that no third parties were present when the money changed hands was not significant to the case. According to her, demands for and payments of bribes generally do not take place in public or in the presence of large numbers of people.

Asked whether Mikautadze went directly to the SSS and handed the money to Liluashvili, Berdzenishvili replied: “Yes. According to the witness, that is what happened.”

The prosecutor said the investigation had also questioned other people who had previously visited Liluashvili. According to their testimony, the procedure for receiving visitors was not always the same.

“The witness also described how he entered the relevant office after undergoing a security check and other procedures. Other people who had previously visited Grigol Liluashvili were also questioned about how they entered the building. Security staff recorded the entry procedure and noted that it did not always involve issuing a pass, a search and so on. In other words, the defendant himself decided how visitors would enter his office,” Berdzenishvili said.

According to her, these circumstances and other factual evidence in the case support the reliability of the information Mikautadze provided to the court.

Berdzenishvili said Mikautadze told the businessmen that the money was being handed over in the interests of the state. According to the prosecutor, one of the businessmen also confirmed this.

“According to the witness, he told the businessmen that this was being done in the interests of the state. One of the businessmen also confirmed this during questioning. They presented the payment as something that served the state’s interests, although this was merely a formal justification. Of course, it was clear to everyone involved that it did not actually serve any state interest,” the prosecutor said.

Berdzenishvili also confirmed that, according to the investigation, Mikautadze brought the money to Liluashvili’s office in a bag.

“Yes, he had the money in his bag. As for his presence in the building, we questioned a security guard who confirmed that he saw Romeo Mikautadze, for example, on the same floor,” she said.

Journalists also asked the prosecutor whether Romeo Mikautadze could face charges, since he was the person who delivered the money to Liluashvili.

According to Berdzenishvili, the involvement of many people in the case is clear. However, authorities cannot classify a person’s actions as a crime until they launch criminal proceedings against that individual.

“I cannot call it a crime in advance until criminal proceedings have been launched against a particular person. I cannot classify a specific action as a crime — even in the case of Grigol Liluashvili. I am speaking based on the standard of reasonable suspicion. In general, if the case confirms that standard, criminal proceedings may be launched,” she said.

As for Mikautadze providing information to investigators, the prosecutor described it as cooperation. She said the defence was wrong to argue that Mikautadze was cooperating with investigators only to receive certain benefits and that such cooperation itself constituted a crime.

The prosecutor also did not rule out bringing criminal charges against Romeo Mikautadze in the future if investigators find sufficient grounds to do so.

“I did not rule that out. I simply described the situation that the defence presents as some kind of special case. I want to stress that the authorities will address the actions of all those involved, the decisions they made and the extent of their cooperation with the investigation within the framework of the law and justice,” Mariam Berdzenishvili said.

Background

Romeo Mikautadze is a former deputy economy minister. The State Security Service arrested him on 21 June 2025. According to the agency, Mikautadze faced charges of abuse of office and laundering millions of lari in illicit proceeds.

The case initially focused on corruption allegations against Mikautadze. In March 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison. Mikautadze also testified as a witness in the case against Grigol Liluashvili. The prosecution considers his testimony one of its key pieces of evidence.

Grigol Liluashvili headed the State Security Service from 2019 until April 2025. He left his post on 2 April 2025.

Liluashvili was arrested on 23 December 2025 after appearing for questioning at the prosecutor’s office. Investigators accuse him of receiving a particularly large bribe as part of a group acting in a prior agreement. According to the case file, the charges involve several episodes, including two linked to Romeo Mikautadze.

The charges against Liluashvili concern receiving a particularly large bribe. The relevant article carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

Corruption cases in Georgia

World.title: School uniforms return to Georgia’s public schools: what you need to know
World.content:
School uniforms in Georgia

Boys will wear jackets like these to school. Photo: Educational Resources

From the new school year, school uniforms will become compulsory for pupils from first to sixth grade in Georgia’s public schools. Boys will wear dark blue trousers and jackets, while girls will wear jackets made from the same material and skirts. The uniforms were made in China and consist mainly of synthetic materials.

The Education Ministry spent more than 45 million lari on the uniforms (approximately $17,226,540,000 — JAMnews). However, the uniforms will not be free for pupils, as parents will have to buy them from the government. Only children from socially vulnerable families will receive free sets.

The ministry says standardised uniforms will reduce social differences and strengthen pupils’ sense of belonging to their schools. However, some parents question the need for compulsory school uniforms. Their main concern is whether it makes sense to prioritise uniforms when more pressing problems with school infrastructure, safety and food remain unresolved.

Questions have also been raised about the quality and comfort of the uniforms. How comfortable will they be for young children? Will they be able to fasten the buttons and zips themselves? Will they be too hot in summer or too cold in winter?

Why has the school uniform become compulsory? How safe is the fabric used to make it for children’s health? Why did the government choose a Chinese company when Georgia also has a developed textile industry? What exactly will standardised uniforms change in Georgia’s troubled education system?

Why has the ministry decided to bring back school uniforms?

In September, six-year-old Ilia will begin a new stage of his life — he is starting school. Ilia attended kindergarten, but adapting to a new environment and stricter discipline will still be a challenge for him.

Ilia will face another challenge — running and playing during breaks in a polyester jacket and tight-fitting trousers.

“My son is used to wearing clothes made of cotton or wool with a small amount of elastane. Until he was six, he did not even wear jeans because they were not stretchy enough. I do not know how he will be able to run around in this jacket during school activities. And I wonder whether it will even stay on him. I doubt that restrictive clothing, against the backdrop of the stress of adapting to school, will help a child develop a sense of belonging to school life,” says Ilia’s mother, Taya Maharashvili.

Taya plans to contact the Education Ministry and demand stronger justification for making school uniforms compulsory:

“I have never opposed introducing a dress code. I believe it is important to dress appropriately in educational and professional environments, and children should learn this from an early age. However, the uniform proposed by the ministry is unacceptable.”

Introducing school uniforms for pupils in the lower grades of public schools is one element of a planned large-scale education reform. Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the measure on 2 December 2025 during a presentation of the National Concept for General Education Reform.

“School uniforms will help create an environment focused on learning and foster a sense of belonging to the educational institution. They will also reduce visible differences in pupils’ socio-economic backgrounds,” Mikanadze said.

School uniforms were compulsory in Georgia in the past. In Soviet schools, pupils wore dark brown, black or blue uniforms with white aprons. In independent Georgia, only some private schools require uniforms, although parents there have also complained about the quality of the fabric.

Polyester, viscose and elastane — what materials are used to make the clothes?

School uniform design. Photo: Education Ministry

The appearance, colour and quality of the school uniforms were determined entirely by the state. The boys’ uniforms will be plain dark blue, while the girls’ uniforms will feature a checked pattern. The state emblem will appear on the left side of the jacket.

The uniforms are made mainly from synthetic materials: 72% polyester, 25% viscose and 3% elastane.

The jackets will also have polyester lining. According to ministry documents, only the skirts will have cotton lining.

The uniforms can be washed at 40°C and ironed at 110°C. Bleach is prohibited, as is ironing the emblem or dry-cleaning the garment.

The school uniform set will include a jacket and trousers for boys, and a jacket and skirt (or a jacket and trousers) for girls.

“First of all, this uniform is uncomfortable. It reminds me of a situation where a paediatric dietitian insists that a child eat vegetables, only for the child to spit them out. I have the feeling that the ministry employs people who have no idea what children and childhood are like,” Taya says.

One uniform set will cost 95 lari. Some pupils will receive it for free.

Trousers and skirts will cost 25 lari, while a jacket will cost 45 lari. A set may include a jacket and two pairs of trousers, or a jacket, trousers and a skirt. As a result, one school uniform will cost parents 95 lari.

Most parents say one set will not be enough for a child to wear throughout the week. Pupils will also need a white shirt or T-shirt under the uniform, which parents will have to buy separately.

Pupils from socially vulnerable families will receive uniforms free of charge. This applies to families registered in the Unified Database of Socially Vulnerable Persons with a rating score below 65,001.

Children in state care or foster families, as well as those living in family-type homes or shelters for children without parental care, will also receive uniforms free of charge.

Ukrainian pupils who have been living and studying in Georgia since the start of the war will also receive school uniforms free of charge.

Is the uniform fabric safe? What should parents do if their child has an allergy or skin condition?

Third-grader Sandro has urticaria and allergic dermatitis. That is why his mother, Sopho, who is raising him alone, pays close attention to the quality of his clothes.

“My son is at school from 9:30am until 6pm, and I am concerned about everything: the quality, comfort and presence of allergens,” says Sopho Trapaidze.

Polyester, the material used for the uniforms, is widely used in the textile industry because it is durable and inexpensive. However, doctor Eka Kvirkvelia notes that the material is not suitable for everyone and is not hypoallergenic for all people. In some cases, it can contribute to overheating, increased sweating and skin irritation.

“True hypoallergenicity depends not only on the composition, but also on the fabric’s breathability, the chemical composition of dyes, production standards and the lining material. It is also important to understand that ‘international practice’ does not mean there is a single standard: different countries use different approaches. Nevertheless, natural fabrics or materials with a high cotton content are often preferred for primary school pupils,” she wrote on social media.

According to her, assessing the quality of school uniforms should rely on specific indicators, such as the percentage of each component, dermatological test results and data on children’s safety, rather than broad claims such as “hypoallergenic”.

Taya Maharashvili has also begun looking at practices in other countries. Polyester is used in schools in some developed countries, but there is one important detail:

“The percentage of polyester in our school uniforms is higher than in those countries. In addition, such countries more often introduce a dress code rather than a uniform. How the fabric has been treated and whether it meets safety standards are also important. They say these factors were taken into account when the Georgian school uniform was designed. However, the public should demand more reliable information supported by evidence, such as expert assessments and so on.”

Education Ministry says exceptions will be allowed

Parents are already demanding additional evidence from the Education Ministry that the fabric meets safety and quality standards. They are also calling on doctors to help address the issue.

“We demand a change in the fabric used for school uniforms. Synthetic clothing is harmful to children’s health,” Tamuna Gagnidze writes.

Dozens of parents have left comments under her post making similar demands. Many say they do not intend to dress their children in the uniforms.

“My child cannot wear polyester: he has atopic dermatitis, and contact with this material makes his skin worse. I absolutely do not want the school uniform to cause bleeding wounds on his skin,” says Hatuna Laghadze in a comment.

Sopho Trapaidze also does not plan to buy a new uniform for her son Sandro. She plans to make it herself — in the same style and colour, but from higher-quality material.

The Education Ministry says it will take into account cases where pupils have officially confirmed medical contraindications.
