World.title: The same thing killed 43 per cent of these astronauts. Scientists have a theory
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCardiovascular health The same thing killed 43 per cent of these astronauts. Scientists have a theory Angus Dalton August 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. You’re reading an excerpt – sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox. A 2016 study reached a shocking conclusion for those who dream of space travel: going to the moon might cost you your heart. Researchers wrote in Scientific Reports that 43 per cent of the Apollo astronauts who travelled beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field, exposing themselves to the harsh radiation of deep space, had died of cardiovascular disease. Space agencies and Elon Musk are aiming for long-term space missions. Human hearts may not cope. Aresna Villanueva For astronauts who went only to low-Earth orbit and didn’t fully leave the “magnetosphere”, the rate of death from heart disease was 11 per cent.



The authors concluded astronauts who went to the moon were four to five times more likely to die from heart disease. This risk calculation was heavily disputed, with an obvious limitation being the tiny sample size of Apollo astronauts who had died at the time (seven). Follow-up papers argued the risk assessment was skewed because researchers didn’t properly account for risk factors such as age, and the fact one of the astronauts had existing heart issues separate to his exposure to deep space. Nevertheless, the research focused attention on an indisputable problem: the radiation-lashed, zero-gravity wilderness of space exerts dangerous pressure on our soft, Earth-adapted mammalian bodies. An animation of Earth’s magnetic field protecting the planet from a blast of radioactive solar wind. NASA GSFC/CIL/Bailee DesRocher The Apollo astronauts and the recent Artemis II lunar visitors were only beyond the Earth’s magnetosphere for a matter of days.



As the ambitions of Elon Musk, the Australian Space Agency and NASA shift to long-term lunar habitation and travel to Mars, knowing whether the body can cope with months-long deep-space missions has never been more critical. One of Australia’s leading cardiologists, having investigated just that issue, found the effects of such missions could be catastrophic. A contentious paper estimated the Apollo astronauts were four to five times more likely to die from heart disease. Getty Images Reproducing galactic rays “An enormous amount of effort and money and resources has gone into developing the hardware and rocketry to get humans into space, whether it’s SpaceX, Blue Origin, or NASA’s Artemis missions,” says Professor Jason Kovacic, chief executive of Sydney’s Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute and life-long space nerd.



“Far, far less attention has been paid to the human body and what that’s going to have to endure.” Put another way: what’s the point of billion-dollar rockets if all the crew are toast? ‘Galactic cosmic rays tear straight through the side of spaceships.’ Professor Jason Kovacic With collaborators at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York, Kovacic co-led new research in Clinical and Translational Medicine scrutinising how our hearts might fare on a long-term mission to the moon or Mars. Space radiation, he says, emanates from stars and blasts from supernovae that have strewn the universe with a deadly web of galactic gamma rays.



Earth’s stewing molten core thrusts out a magnetic field that shields us from this cosmic lashing. Only 28 people have travelled beyond it (24 Apollo astronauts and four from Artemis earlier this year). Professor Jason Kovacic is chief executive of the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute and a life-long space nerd. Wolter Peeters Spacecraft provide only partial protection from the radiation. “Galactic cosmic rays tear straight through the side of spaceships,” Kovacic says. “It is possible to shield from it, but it requires very thick lead, and putting that kind of quantity of lead in a spaceship makes it too heavy to actually put in space.” Previous studies have replicated space radiation using a single-ion beam generated using one element. Real space radiation is much more complex and high-energy, stemming from a raft of elements including hydrogen, helium, iron and uranium.



To better replicate long-term exposure to space radiation, the researchers used NASA’s Space Radiation Laboratory on Long Island, which replicates the radiation from a range of those elements in space. Some mice were exposed to the radiation. The Artemis II astronauts were the first people in half a century to travel beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field in their April lunar flyby mission. AP “That was very carefully crafted by the NASA engineers to represent a physically and biologically relevant exposure that would realistically mimic long-duration deep space missions,” Kovacic says. Key artery lining ‘obliterated’ Kovacic scrutinised the hearts of the mice more than a year later. A key protective lining of their arteries had been “obliterated”.



“The profound findings are that after we irradiated these mice and watched them for 16 months, the endothelium, which is the lining cells of the blood vessels, was basically stripped bare in the arteries.” Mice are more resilient to clotting than humans, he says. If we lost this protective lining, clots would probably form quickly in our arteries and vessels. A control dummy (foreground) and a dummy strapped with a 26kg trial “AstroRad” vest in the uncrewed Artemis I Orion spacecraft. NASA/Glenn Benson “At the extent we saw the endothelium stripped, that would cause widespread clotting, which would likely be fatal.” The small pilot study had a tiny sample size of less than a dozen mice. “We don’t know how transferable [the results] are [to astronauts],” Kovacic says, adding the research needs to be repeated and expanded.



Related Article Analysis

Space Nuclear-powered villages could be on the moon within 10 years. Where do we fit in? “But if something like this were to happen in humans, it would be catastrophic. And the stakes are high. It’s not like one person may be affected and the rest of the crew won’t. It’s likely that the whole crew would be affected.” The radiation had also increased and destabilised artery-clogging plaque, casting serious doubt on whether the human body could really sustain long-term space travel without serious leaps forward in cosmic exploration technology and spacecraft design. As the Space Race 2.0 accelerates, space agencies are investigating radiation-repelling shelter designs. Lunar colonies may have to live underground. Meanwhile, researchers this week reported the test results of a 26-kilogram protective space vest. The “AstroRad” vest was strapped to a dummy and sent around the moon during the uncrewed Artemis I mission; radiation monitors showed it could reduce the radiation dose of severe solar storms by 40 to 60 per cent.



The Artemis II crew also ferried vials of their own bone marrow to the moon and back to see how the cells warped in space, possibly giving us new insights into cancer treatments. Says Kovacic: “We’ve got a lot of work to do to really understand the effects of longer duration space missions into deep space before we go blasting off to Mars.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Jenny was killed 100 metres from home. The driver was fined $2000
World.content:
Jenny died near her home after being hit by a car in 2024. Pictured with son Daniel and husband Steve.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was a clear August afternoon in 2024, and Jenny Hombsch was making her way home after visiting a neighbour. Despite having a hip injury, Jenny loved to walk around her suburb of Baxter, on Melbourne’s Mornington Peninsula – often taking the family’s dog, Ollie, out twice a day. Since retiring, there was also more time for travel. She and husband Steve were in the midst of planning a caravan trip across the country. But the couple never made it on that trip. Just 100 metres from home, a car exiting the nearby freeway struck Jenny, 68, as she was crossing the street. Paramedics arrived quickly, but she died a short time later. The driver involved in Jenny’s collision was fined $2000 and received a six-month licence suspension. Penny Stephens Jenny’s son, Daniel Hombsch, said his mother was a kind, caring and selfless person. Raised on a farm near Adelaide, she later moved to the Mornington Peninsula with her husband to raise Daniel and his brother, Michael. “She was a very determined, very stoic woman … I was very blessed to have really good parents, especially Mum,” Daniel said. “My brother and I were probably the most significant thing to her. And she always put us first.” In 2025, the driver involved in Jenny’s death pleaded guilty to a single charge of careless driving of a motor vehicle. She was eventually fined $2000 with a conviction in the Frankston Magistrates’ Court and had her licence suspended for six months.



The woman behind the wheel – who was 64 at the time of the crash – wasn’t impaired by drugs or alcohol, she wasn’t using a phone, and wasn’t speeding. The court found she had simply failed to operate her vehicle with the care and attention expected of a reasonable person. The maximum penalty for a first offence of this kind in Victoria is $2509, rising to $5227 for any subsequent offences. The offence does not carry a prison term or mandatory licence disqualification, although a magistrate can suspend or cancel a driver’s licence. Nor can the maximum fine be increased when careless driving results in a death. Daniel, now a lawyer who works at a community legal centre, understands the driver didn’t intend to hit his mother, but, years later, he still struggles to accept the sentence. “Regardless of the victim’s age or gender or what they did for work or their personal circumstances, I don’t see how it can be just to put a $2000 cost on someone’s life,” Daniel said.



Careless driving that results in death is distinct from the more serious offences of dangerous driving causing death or culpable driving causing death. A person found guilty of dangerous driving causing death faces a maximum of 10 years’ prison, while someone found guilty of culpable driving causing death can be sentenced to a maximum of 20 years. “There’s nothing to fill the gap between the standard careless driving offence – as it stands now – and dangerous driving causing death,” Daniel said. “The magistrate needs to have the discretion to sentence something greater than a fine.” Michael and Jayde Davey leaving the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court in 2025. Their son, Jack, was killed by a driver in 2024. Penny Stephens This sentencing gap attracted statewide attention in September 2025, when a driver was fined $2000 over a crash a year earlier that killed 11-year-old Jack Davey while he was at school. Jack’s parents Michael and Jayde were outspoken about the need for legal change outside the Magistrates’ Court after the sentence was handed down, calling the current laws inadequate and inappropriate. Jack Davey, 11, died after the crash at Auburn South Primary School in Hawthorn



In July, the Victorian government announced a large-scale review into the state’s dangerous driving laws, which will be carried out by the Victorian Law Reform Commission. The terms of reference included the consideration of a potential “mid-tier” offence for driving that does not meet the threshold to be considered dangerous, but still results in death or serious injury. Law Institute of Victoria criminal law section chair Jarrod Behan said the review would examine whether the current penalties for offences like careless driving align with community expectations and allow for judicial discretion. Magistrates are faced with a difficult task when handing down sentences for careless driving offences that result in death or serious injury. Wayne Taylor “The review could lead to changes if it finds that Victoria’s current laws do not adequately deal with cases where careless driving – or other forms of dangerous driving – causes death [or] serious injury,” he said. Other states have specific offences carrying significantly higher penalties. In New South Wales, a first offence of negligent driving causing death carries maximum penalties of a $3300 fine and 18 months in prison. In Western Australia, careless driving causing death or grievous bodily harm holds a maximum penalty of $36,000 and/or three years in prison, as well as at least three months of licence disqualification.



Because Victoria has no separate offence for careless driving causing death or serious injury, relevant sentencing statistics are also difficult to isolate. The latest data from the Sentencing Advisory Council show 8999 careless driving charges were finalised in the Magistrates’ Court in the three years to June 2023. Behan said the current laws also limited the sentencing options available to judicial officers. While magistrates and judges have greater sentencing discretion for more serious offences like dangerous driving or culpable driving, the lower maximum penalty for careless driving limits the sentences available. Jenny’s son Daniel called the Victorian Law Reform Commission review into dangerous driving “a great first step”. Penny Stephens “It’s trite to say that these types of cases are very difficult and tragic for all involved,” Behan said. “Often, it’s the case that there’s no allegation that the driver intended to cause any harm. There is rather a moment of inattention or another careless act which leads to a tragic outcome.”

World.title: Swans declare players ‘in serious breach’ of standards as club suspensions loom
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have declared a group of players “are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards” as the club’s board meets on Tuesday night to decide on punishments over their conduct in Melbourne on late Sunday night into early Monday morning. The development comes after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon suggested the players could also face AFL sanctions irrespective of the outcome of an ongoing police investigation into a sexual assault allegation. Loading “The Sydney Swans can confirm that the club board will meet tonight to agree on player sanctions and penalties, now that the club has concluded its interviews with all the players involved in the incident in Melbourne,” the Swans said in a statement. “We respect there is an ongoing investigation by Victoria Police and any actions we take are independent of this.”



The Swans said it was appropriate “to take firm action” and highlight that any sanction they take as a club relates “solely” to club’s standards of expected behaviour. “The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount,” the Swans’s statement read. “The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.” The group of five players, who had remained in Melbourne on Monday behind the rest of the team as it travelled back to Sydney, attended separate meetings with senior club and team officials away from Swans headquarters after driving home to NSW.



The meetings were to discuss the events of Sunday night and Monday morning, which led to a police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. The investigation is being handled by Victoria Police’s sexual crimes squad. “The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning,” Dillon said in a league statement. “The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected,” he said. “Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light.”



This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon and Chad Warner after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. This masthead is not suggesting any of the players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with inquiries. This masthead also contacted a representative of Swan Nick Blakey, who denied Blakey was involved in the incident. But the representative confirmed Blakey had also remained in Melbourne with his four teammates. Clockwise from left: Swans players Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard Earlier on Tuesday, two senior competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the players would be dealt with under the AFL rule that covers bringing the game into disrepute and conduct unbecoming.



- Matt Golding However, late on Tuesday the league said that rule would not immediately be applied. The players had been out drinking after Sunday night’s win over Essendon and returned to the team hotel in the early hours of Monday. The AFL has the power to suspend them under rule 2.3A, which prohibits conduct unbecoming or likely to prejudice the interests or reputation of the league. Any immediate club or league action would be separate to the Victoria Police investigation.



A source close to the group of Swans players, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the players had been fully co-operative with the police probe. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation They said all five had been prepared to speak with police on Monday, but only one was ultimately quizzed. Police told the group they were not ready to conduct a formal interview or speak with any of the players acting as witnesses. The source said leading Melbourne criminal lawyer Tony Hargreaves was called in to assist the group before they were told they were free to leave and return to Sydney.



No player has been arrested and the AFL’s disciplinary action does not make any finding in relation to the allegation that remains under investigation by police. Instead, the AFL and the club have been examining the conduct of the players before and around the alleged incident, and whether their behaviour fell sufficiently below the standards expected of AFL footballers to warrant sanction under the league’s broad disrepute provisions. One of the most recent examples of an AFL suspension under this rule was for then Bulldog Bailey Smith, who was found guilty of conduct unbecoming and suspended for two matches in 2022. Smith admitted to using an illicit substance late in 2021. This masthead contacted all 36 of the Swans’ corporate partners. None were willing to comment on the incident, and so far, there is no indication any of the club’s sponsors will be walking away.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans However, a spokesperson for Origin expressed disappointment. “The club informed us about this incident yesterday, and we are incredibly disappointed. While the matter is subject to an investigation, it is not appropriate for us to comment any further,” the spokesperson said. The Swans players are now facing the prospect of missing not only Sydney’s final home-and-away match against North Melbourne on Sunday, but at least part of the Swans’ finals campaign. Sydney have already secured second position on the ladder and a home qualifying final. Any multi-game suspension would carry significant consequences for the club’s premiership aspirations. The Swans were forced to remain in Melbourne on Sunday night because Sydney Airport’s curfew prevented the team from returning home following its convincing win over Essendon at the MCG.



Several players subsequently went out drinking before returning to the Pullman, where the team and its staff were staying. Police attended the hotel on Monday after receiving the report of an alleged sexual assault.

World.title: A handful of Swans players wanted to keep partying. The fallout has rocked the AFL
World.content:
Swans players were filtering back to the Pullman hotel, the former Hilton overlooking Yarra Park, in the hours after midnight. A handful of current players who had been out until early Monday morning wanted to keep partying back at the hotel. They duly moved to a player’s room. Swans coach Dean Cox and CEO Matthew Pavlich. Michael Howard At one stage, a former Swans player and a further friend joined the group for at least a period of this night. After 2am – the exact timeline is difficult to ascertain even from the multiple sources who spoke to this masthead on condition of anonymity – one of the players made a phone call. Soon afterwards, two women arrived at the Pullman to join the party of several of the players.



It is uncertain what happened next, except that an allegation was soon made by one of the women of a sexual assault. The two women left the hotel room and were joined by a third woman in the foyer, where there was a commotion. After the alleged incident, police were called. The allegation will be the subject of police investigations, as Victoria Police probe the incident. The allegation has been handed to the sexual crimes squad. The five players who remained in Melbourne during the early stage of the police investigation as the rest of the team returned to Sydney on Monday were: Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, plus ex-Demon and tagger James Jordon and mature second year defender Riley Bice.



This masthead has contacted their representatives. This masthead is not suggesting any of the players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with inquiries. On Monday morning at least one senior team official went down to the foyer while the five players who had been in the room with the women were instructed to return to or remain in their own rooms as police began working through the first moments of an investigation that would shake the Swans and the entire AFL ecosystem. There is no doubt that the players will not play this weekend in what is a dead rubber anyway against North Melbourne, but the expectation of close observers – not the Swans – is that the five will miss a bare minimum of two matches. The penalty is almost certain to be uniform.



The Swans are working with the AFL on the matter, but the AFL’s integrity boss, former detective Tony Keane, has remained at arms’ length. The league has left the questioning to the Swans and, in time, to police. On Monday, the five players drove back to Sydney, separately from the rest of the team and travelling officials, in at least two rental vehicles. Sydney Swans players (from left to right) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey. Artwork: Michael Howard By Tuesday, as club and competition confronted arguably the most damaging episode the Swans have faced since their breadline days in the early ’90s, the five would be interviewed by Sydney’s senior management, one by one. They had not been formally interviewed by police, as suggested, but police had spoken to some and advised that they would be in touch down the track. A representative of Blakey’s says that the star running defender did not speak to the police even informally.



Heeney went down to the police headquarters in Melbourne on Monday, in what turned out to be an unnecessary trip, as he was not interviewed then either. Clearly, the police had to gain witness and/or victim statements from the women before they sought answers from the players, as a matter of process. After the Sunday twilight game victory over Essendon, the club had been forced to stay in Melbourne because of the early curfew at Sydney airport. Swans players and officials went out for drinks after the late game. Senior coach Dean Cox as well as a number of the players were on film outside the Harlow, a bar in Church Street Richmond and, according to one witness, about 15 players – Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon among them – went on to the trendy Queen Street bar, Her. They were, the source said, there until close to 2am. It is not unusual for Sydney players to go out for a drink after the game, according to club insiders. The Swans, who have a mature team, tend to trust their players and especially team leaders to exercise good judgment.



Cox was back at the hotel shortly after he left the Richmond bar, not long after midnight according to CCTV footage shown on Seven. The Swans’ hierarchy - led by new chief executive Matthew Pavlich and their chairman Andrew Pridham - were unsurprisingly described as “filthy” with the reckless decisions in those wee hours, irrespective of whether the matter proceeds into a serious criminal charge or not. Confronted by the media avalanche on Tuesday morning outside the club, Cox said he was “obviously extremely disappointed with what’s happened”. AFL CEO Andrew Dillon who had hitherto been silent on the scandal on Tuesday night released a statement that foreshadowed strong action. “Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season,” Dillon said.



“Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us. “Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.” With Cameron Houston Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Canberra, you have a (gambling) problem
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Canberra, you have a (gambling) problem August 18, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ONLINE GAMBLING Well, it is now official. The average IQ of federal parliament’s Labor and Coalition MPs cannot be particularly high.

They both have agreed that problem gamblers will have the option of opting out of gambling advertising or services (″⁣Labor signs off on gambling reform deal with Coalition″⁣, 18/8).

Apparently, no one in either camp can see how stupidly unworkable this option is. One has to despair about our future with decisions of this calibre.

Ross Hudson, Mount Martha Labor had its chance and opted out

Albo, your government will be forever remembered as the government that coulda, shoulda and would have taken decisive action on gambling advertising, but didn’t!

Graeme Martin, Alphington



Gambling not as addictive as anger

Re ‴⁣⁣I can’t stop to save my own life’: Parents read son’s final plea on gambling addiction″⁣, (18/8). Those last words of a young gambling addict who suicided, surely must act to make the Labor government change course and get rid of gambling ads.

We know that’s what the public wants, but it’s not the public that governs. It’s the lobby groups. Nor is gambling, bad as it is, the most dangerous of our addictions. That is anger. Because it is not so obvious.

When Pauline Hanson at the National Press Club said she had always been angry but now Australia has caught up to her views, she was, unfortunately speaking the truth.

The wild west rules of the internet allow disinformation and online abuse to flourish, and when social media algorithms push outrage to keep people clicking on to sell more ads, then some Australians who spend a lot of time on their screens have been trained to be angrier. Under-50s rarely read newspapers, and get all their information on the internet. That cohort will only get larger with time. The federal government has so far been unsuccessful in attempts to protect adults from the harms of the internet and social media.

It has made a start on protecting children and teenagers, but attempts to stop the damage the internet is doing to adult Australians provokes huge pushback from the powerful tech bros and the Trumpist cult in Washington.

That, with the rise of Hanson, is a direct threat to our democracy.

Gary Barnes, Mosman, NSW Clear whose interests are being served

Communications Minister Anika Wells introduced legislation on Monday so that citizens will soon be able to opt out of all gambling advertising.

Given the two options – opt out or opt in – isn’t it obvious whose best interests are currently being served?

Martin Hunt, East Malvern What if I see gambling ads on television?

Labor’s ″⁣opt out″⁣ policy for gambling s obviously cannot apply to television advertising, so it is worthless.

Reg Murray Glen Iris Easy-peasy problem solver

Problem gambler? Opt out of online gambling app. Easy-peasy. Problem solved. Problem drinker? Stay out of bottle shops. Easy-peasy. Problem solved.

Dawn Richards, Huntingdale How many online problem gamblers?

Could someone please get senator Sarah Hanson-Young to tell us how many online problem gamblers there are, and what percentage does this number translate to of the total number of people who gamble online?

Patrick Hennessy, St Kilda



THE FORUM One Nation excise idea

The latest policy idea from One Nation is to cut tobacco excise by 75 per cent, and according to Pauline Hanson, this will “break the black market” (18/8). While this might make for a good headline, it is unlikely to work.

High excise rates have likely contributed to the expansion of the black market, but the market now exists and simply reducing the excise will not make this go away.

Australians who have shown themselves willing to break the law and enable organised crime gangs in search of cheaper cigarettes will likely continue to do this as long as black market tobacco remains cheaper than the legal alternative. And organised crime gangs, having invested heavily in establishing their networks, are unlikely to simply walk away in response to the competition cutting prices.

The illegal tobacco market is a complex problem requiring a thoughtful and multifaceted response. A cut to excise may be a part of such a response, but on its own will do nothing more than increase the profits of tobacco companies while exacerbating our public health challenges.

Simon Bennett, Hawthorn East Hanson’s Trump example

There is no way in the world that Pauline Hanson will ever govern Australia. That is, she and her One Nation party of far-right, conspiracy theorists, science deniers and ignorant xenophobes resemble the presidency of Donald Trump, and after seeing the complete and utter mess he’s created for Americans, and the rest of the world, we certainly don’t want Australia to end up like that.

Henry Herzog, St Kilda East Fauci vendetta

As a retired doctor, I am hoping for a seismic rebellion from the scientific, medical, political, media and LGQBQT communities of the United States against the mean-spirited, self-righteous politicians and administration running the country after Congress voted to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt.

Congress’s persecution of a man who was at the forefront of the fight against AIDS and other community health issues over

50 years of service while at the same time supporting the anti-science stance of their president and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy needs the science world to stand up and scream “enough”.

Social media “influencers”, “bots” and “likes” are no substitute for the hard grinding work of scientific research which underpins truly life-giving advances made in medical and other areas of science in my lifetime.

This outrage must be called out for the appalling political, blame-shifting and personal vendetta it is.

Michael Langford, Flinders Making men’s excuses

What is most appalling about the recent cases of sexual violence against women is not only the behaviour itself, but the attitudes surrounding it.

Ralph Carr has been convicted of rape and sexual assault. Yet, at a pre-sentencing hearing, his barrister reportedly commented on the brevity of the assault, saying: “It must be the shortest incidents of rape that’s come before the courts.“

At Scots College in Sydney, three students have been charged over an alleged sexual assault involving a 14-year-old girl. Comments from some Old Boys appear more concerned with defending the boys and the school than confronting the seriousness of the allegation, even suggesting the girl was a willing participant.

And now the Sydney Swans are embroiled in an allegation of sexual assault.

While there have been no charges as yet in relation to the Sydney Swans incident, and the Scots College students are yet to enter pleas, the recurring theme is disturbing: why are we still so quick to minimise, rationalise or defend men’s behaviour, while the victim is almost an afterthought?

A sexual assault is not less serious because it was brief. A girl does not become responsible for an assault because someone suggests she was “willing”. And, no reputation, institution or sporting career should matter more than the safety and dignity of the alleged victim.

Until we stop making excuses for men and start holding them accountable, little will change.

Sue McNamara, Rye



War time myth

As a daughter of a Japanese POW, I can debunk the myth for your correspondent (Letters, 18/8) that the POW survivors of the horrors of the Japanese camps returned home and got on with life without anger or any of the appalling behaviour we see demonstrated in the post-COVID lockdown period.

The untreated PTSD of my poor dad, who did not have the luxury of psychological, financial and social support, has been horrendous throughout his entire life, has had a lifelong effect on his offspring, and is vicariously passed on from generation to generation.

Ruth Davis, Carrum Pandemic, again

Having read Tony Wright’s article, “These diving dinosaurs have defied death forever. But what now?” (15/8), on the more than probable loss of the gannet colonies to h5n1 bird flu in western Victoria, I reflected on my mother’s favourite saying, “there, but for the grace of God, go I”.

Thinking back to the COVID-19 pandemic when as an island continent, Australians could isolate, both internationally and locally, until vaccines arrived to help the storm blow over.

Sadly for our sentient earth friends, many thousands will see their end, which could have also possibly been our end, too.

Kim Kaye, Surrey Hills Celebrity endorsement

The discussion of scams (“Scams on the rise targeting high-profile Australians”, 17/8) mentions “a celebrity or trusted personality” but celebrities are generally good at a specific skill, sport, music, or they have a partner who is. They are not financial advisers.

Why would anyone invest their life savings on a pretty person who plays a nice person on TV? It’s sad to say but the words attributed to PT Barnum, “There’s a sucker born every minute”, are too true.

Dennis Fitzgerald, Box Hill Yes, electric trucks

Your article, “Productivity push to allow electric trucks on roads 24/7” (16/8) is exciting. Considering the proved advantages electric vehicles have over internal combustion engine varieties in terms of maintenance and operating cost, it is indeed surprising that there has not been more growth in the number of electrically powered trucks on Australian roads until now.

However, recent developments in commercial fleets of electric “last kilometre” delivery trucks and vans would indicate that the Productivity Commission should find fertile ground for the introduction of heavier interstate freight-carrying electric trucks to replace the noisy diesels still doing the job today.

The change can’t come too soon.

John Gare, Kew East Schools’ uneven field

A mate recently took his grandchildren to basketball held at a Catholic college in the Eltham region where he used to teach. Walking around, he was impressed with the infrastructure investment since his teaching days.

I recently went back to my old school, Essendon High (now Essendon Keilor College senior campus), which I left in 1973.

The only infrastructure built in that 53 years? A day-care centre for preschoolers now exists there. Otherwise, nothing. What a level playing field.

Keith Hawkins, Point Lonsdale



Vote grab season

Re ″⁣Tawdry vote grab″⁣ (Letters, 18/8): Labor, like the Coalition, is not immune to a little ″⁣vote grabbing″⁣ itself. They have recently given $4 million to

$5 million to more than 100 community groups that operate in the Suburban Rail Loop catchment.

These unnecessary handouts are not only a poorly disguised attempt to win over many thousands who might criticise this controversial project, but also they could be seen as ″⁣bribing″⁣ many swinging electors to vote Labor at November’s election.

Peter Fagg, Blackburn Poorly served west

Labor is testing electric trains on the Werribee line with trains that are going to be used in the eastern suburbs. Train lines are closed for this testing, and we all get to travel on rail replacement buses.

Western suburbs get a substandard train service in any case with promises of electric trains to Geelong and the recent closure of Champion Road in Newport to remove a level crossing.

Labor has taken the western suburbs for granted for decades, but I think people are fed up. Two growth corridors and infrastructure are groaning under the weight of population growth.

Deborah Senior, Williamstown Breaking Bard

Re your correspondent (Letters, 14/8) who sparked debate with his question, “Would you understand the reports if Shakespeare was reading the news on television?“: Shakespeare may not be seen, garbed in an Elizabethan doublet, ruff and breeches, presenting TV bulletins, “What news, what news in this our tott’ring state?”

However, he’s certainly in the audio department. Shakespeare is “spoken” every day – 90 per cent of his language is still in use, including 1700 words that he is credited with creating, such as eyeball, puppy, gossip, addiction, and blushing, plus many phrases and idioms, including the green-eyed monster, vanish into thin air, fight fire with fire, and love is blind.

His world also has parallels with the present. London and Venice were multicultural centres of international trade and finance (The Merchant of Venice); wars were being fought (Henry V); globalisation was on the map (The Tempest); and sorcery and loss of sanity were subjects of intrigue (Macbeth).

As reinvention goes, from 2009, The Hip Hop Shakespeare Company sets Shakespeare to rap music and takes the Bard to young people. In all, not a bad innings for a man who died in 1616.

Barbara Chapman, South Yarra AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding



Trump world

Trump told the world he had bombed Iran so as to “de-nuclearise” it, whatever that means. Any threat to the world from your friend’s North Korean nuclear arsenal, Donald?

Alan McLean, Queenscliff Simply put, to end the Strait of Hormuz issue, all that needs to happen is for Iran to offer a deal: They’ll toll the Strait; Iran to keep 50 per cent of the toll, the Trump family trust the other 50 per cent. Done, war over, move on.

Tom Stafford, Wheelers Hill Is Elon Musk predicting a world without money because he plans to have it all for himself? (″⁣Why the richest man on Earth wants you to think money won’t matter″⁣, 16/8).

Michael Meszaros, Alphington Furthermore

Re Matt Golding’s Logies cartoon (Letters, 18/8): Our newsagent has been operating in Kyneton for over 100 years. And we still do home deliveries, not by horse or bike, but have moved on to cars.

Lyn Bayley, Kyneton So, alleged perpetrators, often wealthy, can have their identities suppressed for years because of concerns about their mental health. How about the alleged victim’s mental health? Obviously, not a priority.

Marie Nash, Balwyn



The Productivity Commission proposal to allow electric trucks to deliver goods around the clock sounds good. But unless much of the freight is transferred to rail for a major part of the journey, there will be more and larger potholes.

Rod Watson, East Brighton The headline read, ″⁣Labor ignored warnings of surge of Kiwi migration″⁣ (18/8). I thought, ″⁣what’s wrong with New Zealand birdlife coming here?″⁣ Then I realised it was just xenophobia yet again.

John Cain, McCrae If anyone with Point Lonsdale connections can afford a ticket to a night with local MP Richard Marles (CBD, 18/8), could they please seek his assurance that AUKUS really isn’t going to replace the gun emplacements at the Lighthouse Reserve in anticipation of a Chinese invasion?

Norman Huon, Port Melbourne The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: AFL should consider enacting no-fault stand-down policy
World.content:
August 18, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At this early stage there are some things that are known and much that is not about what happened at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel when the Sydney Swans stayed there this past weekend. We know that detectives from Victoria’s sexual crimes squad are investigating an alleged incident from the early hours of Monday morning and that five Sydney Swans players are assisting the police with their inquiries into the matter. Clockwise from left: Swans players Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard Exactly who police are focused on or why we do not know, although The Age has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who remained in Melbourne as the team headed back to Sydney after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. We know the players would also face sanctions at a club and AFL level, outside of the police investigation – likely bans of multiple matches.



Several strands arise from the preceding. First, and most importantly, is the welfare of any alleged victims. In the roar of commentary and speculation, those voices must not be forgotten. Second, is both the reaction and consequent actions of the club, and third, the position of the AFL in such matters. Loading We note with dismay the comments of Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich, who said: “We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own internal inquiries ongoing. It’s safe to say we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation.” Pavlich was shocked and disappointed, which is fair enough. Everyone should be, but to append to shocked and disappointed that “the players have found themselves in this situation”?



This takes club loyalty to a new, and depressing, level, where players are already being rhetorically crab-walked away from their own alleged actions. The Swans have said all options were open in regard to the players’ behaviour and certainly the impact on the second-on-the-ladder club, with the finals just a few weeks away, will be considerable. Instead of a sole focus being on reaching a fifth grand final in just over a decade and then winning it, the club’s campaign has been seriously derailed, even before much is known about the police investigation. Police investigations into alleged sexual assault will take time with the careful gathering of evidence and witness statements. The incident brings into focus the sharp contrast between the NRL and the AFL in dealing with such matters. In 2019, the NRL introduced a no-fault stand-down policy for cases that involved penalties of more than 10 years’ jail.



The policy came into effect in the context of sexual assault charges against player Jack de Belin, who pleaded not guilty. He was out of the game for almost three years, and returned to the field when the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions dropped the charges. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans At the time, Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter Beattie said: “I want to make it clear this is no fault, we’re making no judgment whatsoever, in relation to any player charged with any offence. What we’re doing is setting a benchmark and standard for the game of rugby league.” Of course, the allegation involving the Swans is not at the point where it would apply, but creating it would assist all participants. The arguments of judging each case as a standalone has some merit in that each case is different.



An example is that of Geelong’s Tanner Bruhn, who faced sexual assault charges, who was stood down from the competition for all of last season while the case went through the courts. Bruhn maintained his innocence. The charges were dropped, and he returned to play for the club this year. The NRL justified its introduction of the policy as creating a benchmark. A wider no-fault stand-down policy would lay a similiar foundation for AFL players and clubs, and indeed the public, on which expectations can be built. It would help instil greater confidence at times when it is at its most prized. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: How Vickii transformed a higgledy-piggledy home into an entertainer’s dream
World.content:
PropertyNewsConstruction How Vickii transformed a higgledy-piggledy home into an entertainer’s dream Dan F Stapleton August 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Vickii and James Scott were in no rush to find a new home – but they weren’t expecting the hunt to take three years. “We looked at 500 houses in that time, going to inspections every weekend,” Vickii, a school registrar, says. “We didn’t know exactly what we were looking for; we just knew we hadn’t found it yet.” Vickii and James Scott in their transformed Turramurra kitchen. Ben Symons The couple did have a few criteria. For a start, the home needed to be large enough to host their entire family – two adult daughters, plus sons-in-law and grandkids – during holidays. Ample outdoor space was important, as was proximity to shops and public transport. The pair didn’t want to stray from Sydney’s Upper North Shore, where they had grown up and raised children.



The couple had built their previous two homes, and Vickii was hoping their next purchase would offer a similar challenge. “Building and renovating is in my blood,” she says. “My parents built four homes themselves and my uncle’s a builder. The first thing I do when I walk through a house is think about how I could change it.” The pair in 2019 snapped up a five-bedroom North Turramurra home, paying $2 million. They then embarked on a stylish renovation project and now have decided to sell, as they look towards retirement and prepare for a new chapter. “We knew immediately it was the one,” Vickii says.



After 500 inspections, what made this house stand out? “We loved that it didn’t have a straightforward floor plan: it was a higgledy-piggledy house,” Vickii says. “It also had two fireplaces and the most amazing outdoor entertaining area, plus an enormous pool. It ticked every box.” Still, there was scope to expand the kitchen and reinvigorate the downstairs living spaces. The downstairs living area before it was renovated by the Scotts. Domain “Because it’s a full-brick home on a concrete slab we knew that moving walls and plumbing to redo the kitchen could be expensive,” Vickii says.



“But, to me, the kitchen is the heart of the home. In the end we just went for it.” The work began in September 2023. The kitchen was gutted and rebuilt, with space carved out of a hallway for a large butler’s pantry. The kitchen before it was gutted and completely reimagined. Domain The living room, laundry and downstairs bathroom were all redesigned. One of the two gas fireplaces was transformed into a wood-burner, and fresh living-room cabinetry was built in, creating an elegant display space for heirlooms. An interior-design enthusiast, Vickii was clear on what she did – and didn’t – want the renovation to look like. The existing scheme was plain, with a vague Hamptons influence.



Instead, she devised a material palette to imbue the home with a sense of seriousness and sophistication: slabs of grey-veined Arabescato Borghini marble, blond oak floorboards and burnished-brass cupboard and drawer hardware. In the kitchen, the island base, rangehood and joinery were all painted Black Cockatoo, an almost-black shade of green from Porter’s Paints. Black Cockatoo from Porter’s Paints is a key feature of the kitchen. Ben Symons “It’s dark but it works,” Vickii says, “and when it’s bright outside, the green really comes through.” The couple stayed in the home while work took place as the upstairs rooms weren’t slated for a makeover.



That made staying put easier, although the kitchen overhaul meant there was no water downstairs. “We used a tap outside and cooked on the barbecue, which was an adventure,” Vickii says. The butler’s pantry. Vickii says she loved to cook in the kitchen. Ben Symons The renovation began smoothly. “We had a terrible time building our last house – the builder went broke halfway through,” Vickii says. “Talk about drama. So we planned this one very carefully, to avoid any nasty surprises.”



But as work progressed, the project timeline began to slip. By early December the kitchen was half complete, the high-spec Ilve appliances languishing in their boxes. Related Article Interior design How to choose the ideal colour palette for your home “We had the whole family coming to stay for Christmas and it went right down to the wire,” Vickii says. “I was getting very heated with the builders and they were getting very heated with us.” Finally, on December 23 the job was done, and Vickii was able to test-drive the new kitchen with the family. “It’s a real ‘wow’ kitchen and it’s practical, too,” she says. “I love cooking in it. It’s a happy place.”



The renovation was finished in time for Christmas. Ben Symons Now, after their peaceful years in the home, the Scotts have decided to sell. “It’s time to get rid of the mortgage and retire,” Vickii says. “We are sad to be leaving our street but we are hoping to stay close. North Turramurra is very special. It’s not pretentious and the community is beautiful.” James and Vickii Scott are selling but they have loved their time in the Turramurra home. Ben Symons Listing agent James Levy of Ray White Upper North Shore says the renovation has elevated the home in tightly held North Turramurra.



“It’s rare to find a home with a renovation of this quality. It’s not just a lick and a promise; there’s a level of attention to detail that you seldom see.” Levy is not concerned about selling the home during Sydney’s softer market. “A home like this will stand out in any market. It’s got the quality and the lifestyle that people are looking for but don’t often find.”
